opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the genuinely hard problems right now, and in some ways the field has been slow to adapt to it. For a long time, NLP evaluation was built around fairly static benchmarks: you have a test set, you have gold labels, you compute accuracy or F1, and you climb the leaderboard. That worked reasonably well when the tasks were narrow — parsing, named entity recognition, question answering over a single paragraph. But as models are being used for much more open-ended, multi-step work, that paradigm starts to break down in a few ways.

One problem is just saturation and contamination. Benchmarks get absorbed into training data, directly or indirectly, and models get very good at the particular distribution of the benchmark without that necessarily reflecting the underlying capability. So you see these impressive numbers, and then you put the model in a slightly different situation and it falls over. I think we need to put much more weight on held-out, freshly constructed evaluations, and on measuring robustness — how performance changes under perturbations, rephrasings, and distribution shift — rather than a single headline number.

The second thing is that for complex tasks, what you care about is often the process and not just the final answer. If a model is doing a multi-step research task or writing and debugging code over many turns, you want to know: did it reason correctly, did it use evidence appropriately, did it recover from mistakes, did it know when it didn't know something? A final-answer metric can hide a lot of lucky guessing or shortcut-taking. So I'm a believer in evaluations that look at intermediate steps, and at calibration — does the model's confidence track whether it's actually right?

For world models specifically, I think the key question is whether the model has an internal representation that supports counterfactual and causal reasoning, not just next-step prediction that happens to look plausible. A model can generate very convincing continuations of a video or a scenario while having a pretty incoherent underlying picture of the world. So you want tests that probe consistency: if I intervene on something, does the model's prediction change in the right way? Does it maintain object permanence, physical constraints, the state of other agents' beliefs? Those kinds of structured probes tell you a lot more than whether the output looks realistic.

And then finally, I think we have to take human-centered evaluation more seriously. Ultimately these systems are being used by people to get things done, so some of the most meaningful evaluation is: does working with this system actually make people more effective, do they end up with correct beliefs, do they over-trust it? That's expensive and messy to measure compared with running a script over a test set, but I think it's where a lot of the real signal is. So my overall view is that we need a much more diverse portfolio of evaluations — dynamic, process-aware, robustness-focused, and grounded in real use — rather than hoping a few benchmark numbers capture what matters.

r001.rationale: It contrasts narrow, static component benchmarks with open-ended, multi-step work and says the old evaluation paradigm breaks down for complex tasks.

r002.rationale: It does not mention game designers or the time they need to realize an intended game.

r003.rationale: It discusses whether systems help people and whether users over-trust them, but does not treat users’ model choices as evidence of perceived utility.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the places where the field has gotten itself into a bit of trouble, honestly. For a long time, the way we evaluated language models was essentially benchmarks: you have a fixed test set, you measure accuracy or perplexity or whatever, and you report a number. And that was fine, in a way, when the systems were doing relatively narrow things like part-of-speech tagging or answering trivia questions. But the problem now is that people are using these models for things that are open-ended, multi-step, and where there often isn't a single right answer. If I ask a model to help me restructure a codebase, or draft a grant proposal, or reason through some tricky question in economics, there's no gold label sitting there that tells you whether it did a good job.

So I think a few things have to change. One is that we need to think much more in terms of evaluating processes rather than just outputs. If the model is operating as an agent, doing a sequence of actions over time, you want to know things like: did it make sensible intermediate decisions, did it recover when it got something wrong, did it know when to stop and ask rather than barreling ahead. Those are the properties that actually matter to someone relying on the system, and a final-answer accuracy number mostly hides them.

The second thing is that I think there's a real tension between evaluations that are cheap and reproducible and evaluations that actually reflect what people care about. The reproducible ones get gamed, partly through outright contamination of training data, but also just through the natural dynamics of everyone optimizing for the same leaderboard. And the ones that reflect real use tend to be expensive, involve humans, and are hard to compare across time. I don't think there's a clean solution there, but I'd rather see more effort going into carefully constructed human studies and task-based evaluations, even if they're noisy, than yet another multiple-choice benchmark where everyone's at ninety-something percent.

On the world models side, I'd say the honest answer is that we don't really know how to evaluate them yet, and we should be a little humble about that. There's a lot of talk about whether these systems have an internal model of the world, and people point to things like being able to simulate physics or predict the consequences of actions. But a lot of the evaluations are really testing whether the model has memorized a lot of patterns about how things usually go, which is not quite the same thing. I think the more interesting tests are ones that probe generalization to situations that are structurally novel, where you can't get the answer just from having seen similar text or video before. And that's where I think the connection to language is actually interesting, because language gives you a way to specify and query those novel situations very flexibly.

The last thing I'd say is that evaluation should be tied to what you're actually going to use the system for. There's a tendency to want one universal score, and I just don't think that makes sense anymore. A model that's great at mathematical reasoning might be terrible at understanding the social nuance of an email, and both of those matter to different people. So I'd push for more domain-specific, use-driven evaluation, done carefully, and a lot less reading into aggregate numbers than we currently do.

r001.rationale: It contrasts relatively narrow benchmark tasks with open-ended, multi-step tasks lacking a single right answer, and explains why evaluating the latter requires more than final-answer scores.

r002.rationale: It does not mention how long a game designer takes to realize an intended game as a measure of world-model success.

r003.rationale: It recommends evaluations tied to use cases, but does not treat users’ choices among models as evidence of perceived utility.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to move beyond the idea that there’s one number that tells us how good a model is. A benchmark can be useful, but answering a collection of isolated questions is quite different from helping someone carry out a complicated task over an hour or a day.

For a language model, we should ask whether it understands what the person is trying to accomplish, whether it can use the relevant information, and whether it recognizes when it needs to ask a question. And then, if it makes a mistake, can it recover? In a longer interaction, those things become as important as getting the first answer right.

With world models, I’d particularly want to test predictions about what happens when you act. Can the model anticipate the consequences of an action, and can it revise its understanding when the outcome is different? Producing a plausible description of the world is one thing. Having an understanding that supports successful action is a stronger test.

So I’d want a combination of controlled experiments, where we can diagnose particular capabilities, and evaluations of complete tasks with people. Did the person actually accomplish something? How much supervision did they have to provide? Was their trust in the system appropriate? We should measure the success of that whole interaction, rather than assuming that a higher benchmark score automatically translates into a more useful system.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts isolated questions with complicated tasks, but does not say that benchmarking end-to-end interactive tasks is harder.

r002.rationale: It does not mention how long a game designer takes to realize an intended game.

r003.rationale: It discusses task success, supervision, and trust, but does not treat users’ model choices as evidence of perceived utility.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question has to be: evaluated for what? We often talk as though there ought to be a single number that tells us how good a language model is. But as people use these systems for more complex tasks, what matters is whether they can accomplish the task, how reliably they do it, and how much help they need along the way.

For a world model, in particular, producing a plausible description isn’t enough. You’d like to know whether it can predict what will happen if you take some action, whether it can update its beliefs when it encounters new evidence, and whether those predictions remain consistent over a longer interaction. You need settings where a mistaken understanding actually leads to a different outcome.

And then I think we should evaluate the human and the system together. Does using the model help someone do better work? Can they recognize when it’s wrong? A system that gives a very confident answer and occasionally makes a consequential mistake may be less useful than one that knows when to ask a question or express uncertainty.

So I’d want a collection of evaluations: controlled tests that help us understand particular capabilities, alongside realistic tasks that test whether those capabilities hold together. The harder question is increasingly not whether a model can give a good answer once, but whether you can depend on it throughout a substantial piece of work.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts controlled capability tests with realistic tasks and says sustained dependence is a harder question, but it does not clearly explain that benchmarking effectiveness on end-to-end interactive tasks is harder than benchmarking isolated components.

r002.rationale: It does not mention how long a game designer takes to realize an intended game as a success measure.

r003.rationale: It does not treat users’ choices of which models to use as evidence of perceived utility.
